book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits

chapters.relation: Matthew McCall's introduction argues that VALIS is about the fuzzy line between delusions, reality, and psychological wellbeing, following Horselover Fat through breakdowns and pink-beam revelations, and that Dick's signature theme is the interplay between metaphysics and emotions. It quotes Dick's own statement of affinity for Spinoza's 'Deus sive substantia sive natura' and promises that Spinoza's system supplies the groundwork for Fat's path to emotional liberation, a path that begins with the pink beam and with blobs.

The section recounts Dick's 2-3-74 experience and the eight-thousand-page Exegesis, then uses Fat's Tractatus to teach Spinoza's Ethics through a goo analogy: the blob is substance ('that which is in itself and conceived through itself') while everything in everyday life, including us, exists only as its modes. It concludes that despite what our senses suggest, thinking through the substance-mode distinction shows we are all contained in the blob, so what is true derives from concepts rather than sense experience.

chapters.file: ch108 - The Nature and Origin of the “Mind”.md
chapters.relation: This section reads Fat's cosmology, in which the 'Mind' created the 'Brain' to preserve the memory of its dead sister and left every constituent of the universe partly deranged with grief, against Spinoza's proofs in the Ethics that there is exactly one infinite, uncaused substance, which is why Spinoza calls the blob God or Nature. It stresses Spinoza's necessitarianism: the will is not a free cause, even God had no choice not to create the world, and the actual timeline is the only metaphysically possible one, so on both Fat's and Spinoza's schemes suffering is a built-in metaphysical consequence.

chapters.file: ch109 - The Origin and Nature of Affective Disorder.md
chapters.relation: Using the opening of VALIS, the section explains Gloria's suicide through Spinoza's account of the passions: imagining we are hated without cause breeds hatred, and Spinoza's lone remark on suicide says those who kill themselves are 'impotent in mind,' overcome by external causes opposed to their nature, since our essence just is the conatus, the striving to persist in being. It then itemizes Fat's three tragedies (Gloria's death, the divorce, losing his son) as accumulating external causes that overwhelmed him into his own suicide attempt, and presents his therapist Maurice's 'take responsibility for your own life' as implicitly Spinozan advice.

The section explains Fat's plasmate doctrine, with VALIS a Vast Active Living Intelligence System and Sophia the two-year-old who briefly cures Fat by revealing he is an alternate personality of Philip K. Dick before dying of a radiation overdose. It contrasts this failed miraculous cure with Spinoza's intellectual therapy: since 'in so far as the mind understands all things as necessary, so far has it greater power over the affects,' Fat should process Gloria's death as a necessity he could never have prevented, dissolving his guilt.

chapters.file: ch111 - The Power of the Intellect, or of Fat’s Emotional Liberation.md
chapters.relation: This section argues that although Fat's 'Mind' cosmology, unlike Spinoza's necessitarianism, leaves room for free will, Fat can still borrow Spinoza's therapy: Tractatus entry 29 says we fell through an intellectual error, taking the phenomenal world as real, so he is morally innocent, and Spinoza's concession that we suffer insofar as we are part of nature means suffering can be limited, not eliminated, by understanding its causes. It closes skeptically, noting that monist liberation demands ditching free will, contingency, and self-evident beliefs, so within a monist world 'sometimes it is an appropriate response to reality to go insane.'

Ronald S. Green's introduction connects Dick's last novels to the Gnostic texts of the Nag Hammadi Library, where the material universe arises from accidents, mistakes, and the devices of an imperfect architect ignorant of the true creator. It recounts how the 2-3-74 visions began with a delivery woman's fish pendant and bright rectangular images, and argues that the contradictory retellings across VALIS, Radio Free Albemuth, and the Exegesis support one another the way Gnostic myth does, each an imperfect reflection of a higher truth that ordinary terms cannot express.

The section reconstructs the 1945 discovery of the Nag Hammadi codices and retells the cosmogonies of The Hypostasis of the Archons and On the Origin of the World: Sophia's experiment produces a veil of darkness, the aborted watery chaos, and Yaldabaoth, the blind ruler who declares himself God and shapes Adam from mud as a reflection of a reflection. It shows that Horselover Fat cites Yaltabaoth to a baffled psychiatrist and treats the Library, available in English only from 1977, as confirming rather than shaping his belief that his private insanity mirrors humanity's collective forgetting that we ourselves are divine.

This section explains the Gnostic doctrine of syzygy, necessarily co-existing male-female pairs, including the Gospel of Thomas's claim that Thomas and Jesus are identical twins, and reads Dick's lifelong mourning of his twin sister, dead five weeks after their premature births, as its biographical echo. It then traces syzygic pairings through the VALIS trilogy (Emmanuel and Zina, Herb Asher and Linda Fox, the strangely real-and-unreal Rybys) and argues that per Exegesis entry 32 the unfolding of the world narrates the death of half of a divine syzygy, the tragic motif Dick perpetually re-enacts.

chapters.file: ch115 - Results of the Primordial Rape.md
chapters.relation: The section retells the Gnostic rewrite of Genesis in which the rulers, lusting after the luminous Zoe, defile only the clay replica she secretly substituted, while the real woman becomes the Tree of Knowledge; the instructor reveals the fruit grants gnosis rather than death, and Yaltabaoth's prohibition was itself engineered by the true God to draw attention to the tree. It draws out the consequences (expulsion, toil and childbirth as deliberate burdens, the undefiled bloodline of Seth and Norea) and notes a Gnostic parallel to Deckard's sexual aggression in Blade Runner.

This section argues that Dick's handling of the pink light enacts the Gnostic conviction that salvation comes from direct inner revelation rather than faith, sacraments, or church, cataloguing his competing theories: transmissions from a VALIS satellite that may itself be Yaldabaoth, mere ruler of the material realm, possession by Elijah, or his being Thomas the twin of Jesus. It weighs Dick's answers to why the true God permits the blind ruler (self-reflection, God's love of games, or our own labyrinth built to see if we could not escape) and the Gospel of Thomas's warning that the divine within will destroy us if we do not bring it forth.

John Sullins's introduction frames evil in Dick as the absence of empathy, noting that in Blade Runner the Voigt-Kampf test exists only because the Tyrell Corporation's replicants mimic every human trait except empathetic response. It argues that Roy Batty and Rachel cross a threshold that puts them in moral parity with humans (Roy's love of life extending to his would-be killer, Rachel and Deckard in love) while many human characters devolve, and poses the chapter's question: what gives a human, robot, or alien moral personhood?

The section reads Dick's first published story, 'Beyond Lies the Wub,' as the origin of his career-defining theme: the jovial, philosophic wub survives the captain who sees only fresh meat because its empathy is so total it can exchange minds with the man about to slaughter it. Defining empathy as seeing the world from another's viewpoint plus sympathizing (which the cornering cat, predicting the rat's moves, lacks), it ends with Dick's Exegesis: an evil magician-deity occludes our minds until a savior in trash form restores them, and without such a revelation you, the reader, are 'nothing but a robot.'

chapters.file: ch120 - How to Tell if You Are Really Just a Robot.md
chapters.relation: Using Imposter's Spence Olham, Rachel in Blade Runner, and 'The Electric Ant,' the section asks how anyone could verify they are not a machine with implanted memories and drives, noting that Dick wrote himself into Garson Poole and re-enacted Poole's drastic self-experimentation in his decades of drug use. It then argues Dick's real criterion is agape, the spontaneous, unconditional love of ancient and Christian philosophy, which robots can simulate but never experience since they love only because programmed: 'You are a robot if you cannot experience empathy.'

chapters.file: ch121 - Can a Blade Runner Love a Robot.md
chapters.relation: The section contrasts Dick's bleaker novel, where J.R. Isadore's love for the androids dies when they cut the legs off his rare spider and Deckard's union with Rachael is the 'summa of falsity and mechanical motions' that fuels his resolve to destroy them, with the film's redemptive romance built on Rachael being 'more human than human.' It argues the movie preserves Dick's thesis anyway: Roy Batty's final act of saving the enemy who hunted him shows the empathy that makes the replicants persons, perhaps more than human.

chapters.file: ch122 - How to Build a Moral Robot.md
chapters.relation: This section draws design morals from Dick's warnings: machines built as ersatz humans deny the value of being human, robotic sexual partners are doomed deceptions (the novel's Deckard-Rachael encounter is the case study), and a genuine artificial moral agent needs empathy 'logically equivalent to agape,' though a machine reasoning on sound moral principles could still count as a limited moral agent with proportionate rights and responsibilities. The Three Stigmata's Palmer Eldritch, returned from deep space as a machine treating humans as resources, shows that the netherward pull toward machinehood threatens humans themselves.

chapters.file: ch123 - PUBLIC RELATIONS GUIDE FOR NEW OFFICERS DIVISION OF PRECRIME.md
ch124 - 01. Don’t We Arrest Innocent People.md
chapters.relation: Writing as a Precrime PR manual, the section answers the charge that arresting people who have broken no law punishes the innocent: pre-criminals genuinely lack mens rea, so punitive blame would be inappropriate, but their detention is justified as prophylactic quarantine, like isolating an infant with a dangerous contagious disease, under a non-punitive containing attitude. It cites Dick's own 'Minority Report' language of 'neutralizing' Anderton and 'the prophylactic pre-detection of criminals,' plus the film's Hall of Containment, as evidence the system is preventive rather than punitive.

chapters.file: ch125 - 02. But Is It Really Inappropriate to Punish Pre-criminals.md
chapters.relation: The section defends punitive attitudes toward pre-criminals through a 'pre-punishment' thought experiment: if Walter Wrath credibly announces tomorrow's wrongful harm and will escape all future blame, punishing him now is better than never blaming him at all. Precrime cases are analogous, it argues, because being stopped by others is no credit to the offender and not the right kind of fact to exculpate him; the person who would have done it 'remains on the hook.'

chapters.file: ch127 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: The section argues Precrime needs no evidence of an actual murder, attempt, or plot because pre-criminals are charged with future-murder, which, unlike plots that fizzle or attempts that bungle, always succeeds absent intervention. Using Anderton's demonstration of Witwer's caught ball, it distinguishes a person's NA-future (if not arrested) from the A-future (if arrested), concluding that what happens after an arrest cannot falsify an NA-prediction, since the prediction only ever described the uninterfered-with path.

chapters.file: ch128 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: This section rebuilds the evidential case for the precogs from their verified early track record, which was free of errors of commission (predicting murders that never happened) and omission (missing murders that did). The still-zero present-murder rate rules out omissions, and cases like Howard Marks, caught mid-attempt, form a random and representative sample of the precogs' predictions showing commissions have not crept in, since arrest-timing delays correlate with nothing systematic about guilt.

chapters.file: ch129 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: The section concedes that Precrime techs erred in the Anne Lively case, failing to notice that some previsions showed ripples moving toward the shore and others away. But it argues this is only the general problem of interpreting any evidence, from confessions to forensics to eyewitness reports, and that human fallibility does not imply unreliability, any more than fallible traditional policing meant murders should go uninvestigated.

The section weighs leaking predictions to pre-criminals so they can reroute (the I-future), and rejects it for three reasons: the precogs' predictions are accurate only for people who never learn of them, standing by to catch a forewarned killer is costly, and would-be murderers have no right to know, since unlike a citizen facing contaminated water they could have avoided their path by not choosing it. It closes the guide's case that Precrime arrests people who deserve arrest, with appropriate attitudes and compelling evidence, without violating rights.

chapters.file: ch131 - Chapter 20 - If the Universe Isn’t Real, How Should We Treat Other People.md
chapters.relation: Andrew M. Butler's introduction opens with the ambiguous endings of Total Recall, Minority Report, and Blade Runner (the fade to white, the too-neat reunion, the improbable sunset) to pose skeptical doubt about whether any of Dick's realities are real, surveying Eye in the Sky, Flow My Tears, Time Out of Joint, and Next. Against the thought that if nothing is real nothing matters, it sets Eric Sweetscent returning to his failing wife, and introduces Dick's aim to fuse Hebrew monotheism with Heidegger's philosophy of thrownness, noting that Levinas made the attempt first and that for Dick the authentic human is the one who cares for others.

chapters.file: ch132 - To Be or Not To Be—Is That the Question.md
chapters.relation: The section introduces Levinas (Heidegger's student, Nazi internment camp survivor, Talmudic scholar) for whom ethics outranks ontology ('To be or not to be? Is that the question?'), and illustrates his strange distinction between existents and existing through Dick's existing-without-existents: the hallucinated town of The Cosmic Puppets, the aura of fake American relics in The Man in the High Castle, Freck's nonexistent aphids. Working through phenomenology, the idios kosmos / koinos kosmos split of A Maze of Death and Eye in the Sky, and the eerie 'There is' of the void, it reworks Descartes's cogito into Levinas's question ('I think, therefore what should I do?') because out there is the Other.

chapters.file: ch133 - He Ain’t Heavy, He’s My Other.md
chapters.relation: This section stages Levinas's infinite responsibility for the Other against Heidegger's tendency to treat others as tools for warding off death: J.R. Isidore's one-way care for androids who vivisect a spider, Dick's 'The Android and the Human' warning that androidization means becoming predictable means, and the treatment of animals as the litmus test of humanity. The self becomes real through selfless action (Tagomi saving a stranger, Sweetscent returning to his wife), and because the height separating self and Other descends from Descartes's idea of infinity, meeting the face of the poor stranger, from Radio Free Albemuth's beggar to The Adjustment Bureau's Chairman, is an encounter with God.

chapters.file: ch134 - Fifty Ways to Love Your Other.md
chapters.relation: The section reads Levinas's demand to experience the Other's suffering in the Other's place as Dick's empathy made literal: the shifting points of view that blur heroes and villains, Felix Buckman's tears, Molinari developing his people's symptoms, and the empathy boxes bonding users to Mercer's endless stoning, a fraud whose falsity is beside the point because the concern is the real thing. Villains are precisely those who refuse the transfer, and the ordinary one-way gift, buying a stranger a drink with no return, enacts the Golden Rule: even if the universe isn't real, Melina is right, kiss each other anyway.

chapters.file: ch136 - Chapter 21 - Knowing Tomorrow While Choosing Today.md
chapters.relation: Sara Worley's introduction frames Minority Report and 'Adjustment Team' as versions of the classic free will problem: if precogs foresee my crime before I commit it, or the Adjustment Team knows what I will do, my action seems already settled, like a sunflower's turn toward the sun. Influence alone does not cancel freedom, since we can do otherwise where plants cannot, but foreknowledge threatens exactly that, the same quandary long posed by an omniscient God who already knows every action we will perform.

The section distinguishes two models of foreknowledge: prediction, as when you confidently predict that sci-fi-loving Jill will skip the John Wayne retrospective, and Molina's 'middle knowledge' of how each person will respond to various circumstances. It then argues prediction can be certain only if character and circumstances guarantee the outcome, the way facts and laws fix where Mars will appear, which would leave no alternatives to choose; so on the predictive model, infallible foreknowledge and the ability to do otherwise cannot coexist.

This section presents the Boethian-Anselmian alternative: God is outside time, so nothing is past, present, or future for him; all events are eternally laid out for him simply to 'look' at, rather than learn about past events from fossils or future ones from predictions. On this model God has no foreknowledge strictly speaking, and his seeing Jill buy her ticket no more constrains her choice than my watching someone choose would make them unfree.

The section tests both models against the stories and finds 'sight' incoherent: the precogs foresee murders that never happen, the Adjustment Bureau tracks two incompatible previsions per circumstance, and a precog genuinely seeing the actual future would generate an oscillating loop in which her own report makes the prevision false. Prediction fits instead: the adjusters tweak Mr. Douglas's cautious character in 'Adjustment Team,' and Anderton's three discrepant predictions in 'The Minority Report' track how leaked information changes his circumstances and motivation to kill Kaplan.

This section argues predictive foresight is compatible with freedom only if probabilistic, yet Precrime treats its predictions as certain, arresting people for what they will rather than might do. Lisa's doubts in 'The Minority Report' turn out to concern incomplete information rather than free will, while The Adjustment Bureau dramatizes freedom differently: the adjusters work by making the preferred path easiest, but David and Elise's three-year persistence shows that those who 'fight' for their free will get it, leaving open how predictable we really are.

chapters.file: ch141 - Chapter 21 - Total Recall’s Total Rethink.md

chapters.relation: The section uses Quaid's Rekall-fabricated life, complete with false wedding memories and a false eight-year marriage, to challenge Locke's memory theory of personal identity: implants, together with ordinary forgetting, revision, and loss, show memory cannot be what makes you the same person from one day to the next. Kuato's line, 'A man is defined by his action, not his memory,' is offered as the alternative the following sections develop.

chapters.file: ch143 - Owning Your Actions, Owning Your Past.md
chapters.relation: This section reconstructs the traditional view of free agency from Aristotle: an action is freely mine when it 'has its origin in the agent himself,' so owning an action means tracing its causal chain back to one's own decision. It explains Aristotle's picture of natures as internal sources of motion and decision as the distinctively human motion, then asks whether Quaid, following the suitcase, video, and clues Hauser pre-arranged, is picking up the chain of his own prior decision, and so becoming himself again.

chapters.file: ch144 - Inpsychation and Chains of Will.md
chapters.relation: The section develops freedom as extending the will through tools and other people, via Nietzsche's 'inpsychation' and Emerson's conversion of fate into force: Cohaagen shuts off the air through Lori and Harry as Hitler invaded Poland through his soldiers. Locke's memory theory returns demoted to a useful tool rather than an identity-maker, and Nietzsche's Genealogy II.1 on the unbroken 'long chain of will' explains Hauser's masterpiece, planning around his own memory wipe so that Quaid, following the planted clues, re-inpsychates Hauser's decisions.

This section complicates everything: two taped Hausers contradict each other, rebel hero or Cohaagen's 'bosom buddy,' so Quaid cannot settle who he is by tracing his origins. It then generalizes: in the scientific worldview of universal causation, from gravity to DNA inherited through chimps and sea squirts from the primeval muck, no one originates anything, a conclusion quoted at length from Baron d'Holbach's System of Nature, yet first-person deliberation still leaves Quaid feeling the weight of choice.

The section rejects randomness as a foundation for freedom, quantum indeterminacy being Epicurus's swerve again, since actions tracing to random particle events are no more mine than law-determined ones, then turns to the ethical problem: if Hauser volunteered and Cohaagen's story is true, freedom-as-origination would require Quaid to become Hauser again, Mercedes included. Quaid's verdict ('The guy's a fucking asshole') shows freedom is also changing course to do what is right; as Lowe says in 'We Can Remember It for You Wholesale,' what defines us is 'not a memory but a desire,' and in breaking with his past Quaid decisively becomes free.

Travis Paterson's introduction reads A Scanner Darkly as Dick's most autobiographical novel and explains Arctor's disgust at the over-happy Brown Bear Lodge audience through Sartre's Nausea: Roquentin's discovery that existence is sheer contingency, that we are superfluous, vaguely alarmed beings who cannot define existence as necessity. Arctor never finds Roquentin's slender chance of acceptance, so the nausea curdles into addiction and the wolf parable, the magnificent lone wolf shot to protect the meager, over-fed animals, poses the chapter's question of why the sensitive outsider is the one sacrificed.

chapters.file: ch148 - Society’s a Bad Hit (If You’re Banging Up, Cranking, or Popping).md
chapters.relation: This section argues A Scanner Darkly's primary philosophical contribution is the recognition that the fate of Dick's drug circle was social violence against those who did not fit in: dominant California normalizes the apathetic, slothful 'straights' of the Brown Bear Lodge while phone-tapping peace advocates, ransacking writers' homes, and hunting or abandoning drug users whose pain gets attributed to addiction rather than rejection. The Thelma Kornford mosquito-hawk episode, the deposition about color TVs, animals, and My Lai, and Donna's final 'It is easy to win' all expose how winning requires never choosing your own values.

This section asks whether the outsider can live in society with dignity, using Charles Taylor's politics of recognition, the claim that dominant societies commit an egregious harm when they refuse to affirm a subculture's value, to read Arctor and his friends as a subculture whose leftover American dream is recognition. Parallels with indigenous ceremonies, typecast immigrant youth, and French assimilation pressure frame the novel's question: can pluralist America include drug culture, or does the ethical order that preaches pluralism have limits the Arctors have already hit?

The closing section rebuts the communitarian defense of California's drug laws, noting there is more than one community and most people belong to several, then turns to Douglas Husak: moral rights exist to protect persons from majority interference, and the crusade against drugs is cultural hegemony. Cocaine, marijuana, and opiates were outlawed along racial lines (blacks, Mexicans, and Chinese respectively) while the ruling class's alcohol and tobacco remained 'autonomous choices,' suggesting the real problem with drugs is who uses them.

holes.name: Gnosticism (gnosis)
holes.what: An ancient religious movement, preserved in the Nag Hammadi library, teaching that the material world was made by an ignorant or malevolent demiurge and that salvation comes through gnosis, direct secret knowledge of our divine origin.
holes.why: Chapter 17 introduces Dick's 2-3-74 visions and the VALIS trilogy entirely through Gnostic texts and their imperfect-creator cosmology, but the taxonomy has no Gnosticism concept to map them onto.

holes.name: Gnosticism (gnosis)
holes.what: An ancient religious movement, preserved in the Nag Hammadi library, teaching that the material world was made by an ignorant or malevolent demiurge and that salvation comes through gnosis, direct secret knowledge of our divine origin.
holes.why: The section's entire exposition, Nag Hammadi, Sophia, Yaldabaoth, and gnosis as immediately certain hidden knowledge, is Gnostic doctrine for which the taxonomy has no slug.

holes.name: Gnosticism (gnosis)
holes.what: An ancient religious movement, preserved in the Nag Hammadi library, teaching that the material world was made by an ignorant or malevolent demiurge and that salvation comes through gnosis, direct secret knowledge of our divine origin.
holes.why: Syzygy, the paired-emanation doctrine used to explain Dick's twins motif and his dead sister, is specifically Gnostic and has no taxonomy equivalent.

holes.name: Gnosticism (gnosis)
holes.what: An ancient religious movement, preserved in the Nag Hammadi library, teaching that the material world was made by an ignorant or malevolent demiurge and that salvation comes through gnosis, direct secret knowledge of our divine origin.
holes.why: The section is a retelling of the Gnostic rewrite of Genesis from The Hypostasis of the Archons and On the Origin of the World, and no existing concept covers this myth.

holes.name: Gnosticism (gnosis)
holes.what: An ancient religious movement, preserved in the Nag Hammadi library, teaching that the material world was made by an ignorant or malevolent demiurge and that salvation comes through gnosis, direct secret knowledge of our divine origin.
holes.why: The section's contrast between salvation by inner revelation and orthodox faith and sacrament, and the identification of VALIS with Yaldabaoth, are Gnostic themes without a taxonomy slug.

holes.name: Baron d'Holbach
holes.what: French Enlightenment atheist and hard determinist whose System of Nature argues that all human actions, like every natural event, are necessitated by prior causes, making free will an illusion.
holes.why: Chapter 145 quotes The System of Nature at length as the definitive statement that in a law-governed nature humans originate nothing, the exact position Quaid must confront.

holes.name: Charles Taylor
holes.what: Canadian philosopher whose politics of recognition holds that identity is formed through social recognition and that dominant societies owe subcultures acknowledgment and affirmation of their worth.
holes.why: Chapter 149's argument that Arctor's friends fight for recognition, and that denying it is an egregious harm, is built directly on Taylor's recognition theory.

holes.name: Douglas Husak
holes.what: American philosopher of law and drug policy who defends a moral right to use drugs and argues that criminalization cannot be justified by any standard rationale.
holes.why: Chapter 150 leans on Husak's critique of drug prohibition as cultural hegemony to answer the communitarian case for outlawing Arctor's subculture.
